sections.title: The bottleneck in software development has moved.
paragraphs: For decades, writing code was the most expensive part of development. Today an AI agent produces in minutes what a team used to produce in weeks. The hard work has moved to two places: defining precisely what is needed, and verifying that what was built meets that need.

Recent research agrees that artificial intelligence amplifies the capabilities an organization already has. Where discipline, specifications and controls exist, it accelerates delivery. Where they do not, it accelerates technical debt and the loss of understanding of the systems.
That is why adopting agents is not a tooling decision but a governance one: who decides, who verifies, and on what evidence.

bars.aria: Comparison diagram. Before: cheap intent, writing code as the bottleneck and verification at human pace. Today: intent and verification are the bottlenecks and agent generation takes minutes.

sections.title: TELAR: the specification as the source of truth.
paragraphs: The Jacquard loom separated the pattern from the machine. TELAR (Spanish for “loom”) applies that principle to software: the specification plays the role of the card, the agent that of the loom, and people retain decisions and verification.
The method establishes a traceable chain linking business intent to every artifact in the lifecycle, all the way to production telemetry.

loops.aria: Nested loops: the business why loop wraps the execution loops where agents work; people govern them from outside, through the harness
loops.caption: The cycle is not a waterfall: people design and improve the harness that governs execution, instead of inspecting every artifact the agents produce by hand.

chain.aria: Chain of intent: INT, REQ, SPEC, TASK, PR, TEST, REL and telemetry, grouped into why and what, how, and evidence
chain.caption: The chain of intent: each artifact links to the previous one and to whoever approved it.

lifecycle.title: A seven-stage lifecycle
lifecycle.text: The intent chain is what remains; the stages are how it is produced. Each stage leaves one or more links of the chain —its number appears above each link— with its controls and its owners. Agents execute; people decide and verify with evidence.

pillars.text: The domain is discovered and bounded with domain-driven design (DDD). Techniques such as Event Storming help explore it and reach a big-picture design.
Specifications anchored to the domain, versioned and owned, that outlive the task that produced them.
Agents work inside a controlled environment (a harness): rules, templates, verifiers and scoped permissions.
Evidence-based controls at every stage. Deciding and verifying are human responsibilities that are never delegated to an agent.
Systems change without losing traceability, and agent autonomy expands only on evidence.

items.q: Some say spec-driven development is dead, or just waterfall again. Why adopt it?
items.a: The debate raises fair points, but it argues about a practice. The underlying need is different: modernizing a software lifecycle designed for a time when writing code was the expensive part, with changes across technology, people, tools and organization. In TELAR the specification is not frozen up front: it evolves with what each delivery teaches and is verified so it does not drift.

items.q: Do we need to change our current tools?
items.a: No. The method is tool-independent: it defines categories and selection criteria. Recommendations are tailored to each organization.

items.q: Does it apply to existing systems?
items.a: Yes. The model includes a specific stage for systems in operation, which are handled lightly while specification coverage grows with use.

items.q: Must every area reach the highest level?
items.a: No. The right level depends on each area’s risk and value. The gap analysis sets the target for each one.

items.q: What happens if the pilot does not deliver the expected results?
items.a: Every phase has a baseline, rollback signals and a stop criterion agreed before starting. Stopping in time is part of the method.

items.q: Do you provide services in English?
items.a: Yes. We serve organizations in Latin America and the United States, in Spanish and English.
